newsitem.title: USA: Judge allows Kevorkian slander suit against AMA.
newsitem.headline: Judge allows Kevorkian slander suit against AMA.

text.p: Dr. Jack Kevorkian scored a victory in his long-running battle with the American Medical Association when a judge ruled on Tuesday that the assisted suicide crusader's $10 million defamation lawsuit against the organisation should go to trial.

Kevorkian attorney Geoffrey Fieger said in press release that he planned to immediately proceed to a jury trial. A spokeswoman for Wayne County Circuit Judge Sharon Tevis Finch said no trial date was set.

Kevorkian filed the lawsuit in February 1996. He accused the AMA of slander and defamation for calling him a "killer" and saying he engaged in "criminal conduct" in comments the group made in October and November 1995.

The 69-year-old retired pathologist publicly acknowledged helping 45 people kill themselves since 1990. Kevorkian defended his role in assisted suicides as humanitarian action intended to relieve suffering.

According to Fieger, Judge Finch said in her opinion that to be accused of being a "killer" could lead to the inference that Kevorkian is a murderer, even though he has not been convicted of the crime.
"This allegation is so strong and so unequivocal that when directed against a specific person, it constitutes libel ... and cannot be considered 'opinion' on a topic of public concern," Finch wrote.
Prosecutors in Oakland County, Michigan, brought murder charges against Kevorkian in the past, but higher courts have thrown them out before they reached trial.
Kevorkian was acquitted at three trials on lesser charges banning physician-assisted suicide. He faces his fourth trial next month in Ionia County, located in central Michigan.

AMA officials at the group's Chicago headquarters could not be reached for comment. At the time the lawsuit was filed, AMA General Counsel Kirk Johnson called it "nonsense." The AMA has been a frequent critic of Kevorkian.
Prosecutors in Ionia have charged Kevorkian with violating the state's unwritten "common law" banning assisted suicide in the August 1996 death of Loretta Peabody.
